market_scan.market_size_text: The underlying installed-equipment market is small but real: global industrial microwave heating equipment sales are ~$1.4-1.6B/yr (2025, ~4-6% CAGR), which implies an installed base of only tens of thousands of machines. The directly addressable software/optimization layer for that installed base is a niche — likely ~$50-200M/yr at best today (~1-10% of equipment spend on simulation/optimization services). The adjacent, much larger context is the process digital-twin market (~$2.6B in 2025, ~31% CAGR), which shows strong operator demand for efficiency software but is dominated by generic platforms without microwave physics.

regions.Europe: ~$0.35-0.45B (equipment market proxy; ~20-30% share, strong density of microwave OEMs and food/pharma users)
regions.Asia: ~$0.5-0.55B (~35% share, largest region per Grand View Research)

market_scan.target_customers_text: Customers are the industrial plants operating installed microwave systems (food tempering/drying/sterilizing, pharma, chemicals, wood, ceramics, rubber vulcanization). SAIREM alone claims ~5,000 machines installed in 70+ countries, so the worldwide installed base is plausibly ~10^4-10^5 machines spread over ~10,000-40,000 plants. Most operators are SMEs with no microwave engineering staff; they are hard to reach directly and are best approached through equipment OEMs, industry associations (AMPERE, IMPI), and retrofit/maintenance channels.

Large: ~45-55% of installed microwave capacity (multi-line multinational food/pharma/chemical operators)

market_scan.players_text: No vendor today sells 'efficiency simulation for existing industrial microwave machines' as a product. The de-facto incumbents are (a) the equipment OEMs' own after-sales/service engineering, (b) generalist EM/multiphysics tools (Ansys, COMSOL, CST) usable only by specialists, and (c) generic digital-twin/APC platforms (AVEVA, AspenTech, Siemens) that lack EM-thermal microwave physics. Niche microwave-heating simulation exists only in QWED's QuickWave heating module and in consultancies/academic groups (e.g., AMPERE network). Competition is therefore fragmented and mostly indirect — the market is essentially unserved as a product category.
players: Large (Ansys/Synopsys, COMSOL, Dassault SIMULIA CST, Siemens, AVEVA/AspenTech)
general EM/multiphysics suites and generic process digital-twin/APC platforms; not microwave-operation specific
~70-80% of EM-simulation spend sits with generalist vendors, but ~0% purpose-built for MW-machine operators
Medium (QWED/QuickWave, solid-state retrofit vendors e.g. RFHIC/LEANFA/SAIREM/Muegge service, specialist MW consultancies)
microwave-heating-capable FDTD simulation, closed-loop/solid-state upgrades, engineering services
Small (independent microwave consultants, university spin-offs, open-source openEMS/MEEP users)
one-off simulation studies, dielectric measurement services, custom in-house models
regulation: Safety standard for industrial electroheating installations using HF/microwave energy (3 MHz-300 GHz): any retrofit or operating-point change must keep leakage and interlock compliance — a simulation product can support re-verification

Limits RF disturbance emissions from ISM equipment; changing operating frequency/power or adding solid-state sources requires re-assessment of emissions — simulation of leakage/harmonics is directly relevant

Microwave process equipment effectively restricted to ISM frequencies (e.g., 915 MHz mainly Region 2, 2.45 GHz worldwide); regional frequency differences constrain which optimization levers (frequency tuning) are legal per market
Sets minimum health/safety requirements for worker exposure to electromagnetic fields; stronger field coupling near machines must be checked when processes are re-tuned
Substantial modification of installed microwave machines (retrofit generators, applicator changes) can trigger re-certification obligations

technologies.name: Multiphysics EM-thermal co-simulation (COMSOL RF+Heat Transfer, Ansys HFSS+thermal, CST Studio)
technologies.how: Full-wave frequency- or time-domain EM solver coupled to heat transfer, iterated as dielectric properties change with temperature; used offline to test what-if scenarios (load geometry, power level, belt position).
technologies.performance: Experimentally validated for applicators (e.g., 915 MHz waveguide vs thermocouple data); single cavity runs take minutes-hours, full parametric sweeps days; expert setup effort measured in engineer-weeks
technologies.limits: Requires scarce EM expertise + expensive seats ($10-70k); accuracy collapses without temperature-dependent dielectric data for the actual product; does not connect to machine telemetry — it is a study tool, not an operations tool

technologies.name: Dedicated microwave-heating FDTD simulation (QWED QuickWave + Basic Heating Module)
technologies.how: FDTD co-simulation with temperature-/enthalpy-dependent media, moving/rotating loads, source-frequency tuning and source switching — the only commercial solver family purpose-built for microwave heating.
technologies.performance: Handles realistic process features (conveyor motion, load rotation, thermal runaway); runs on workstations; smaller vendor so limited global support footprint
technologies.limits: Still an engineering tool needing trained users and per-material dielectric input; no built-in library of operator-facing KPIs or machine templates; minimal presence outside specialist circles

technologies.name: Generic process digital twins / APC platforms (AVEVA, AspenTech, Siemens, Yokogawa)
technologies.how: Plant-data-driven models, energy dashboards and advanced process control applied to thermal lines; the microwave unit treated as a black-box actuator.
technologies.performance: Process digital-twin market ~$2.6B (2025) growing ~31%/yr; proven for furnaces/dryers; delivers ~5-15% typical energy savings in conventional thermal processes
technologies.limits: Cannot model EM field distribution, hot spots or dielectric coupling — the very phenomena that determine microwave efficiency; treat the microwave stage as unmodelled equipment

technologies.name: Solid-state microwave generators with closed-loop control (RFHIC GaN, LEANFA/RFMW, SAIREM, Muegge)
technologies.how: Replace/retrofit magnetrons with LDMOS/GaN amplifiers enabling real-time control of power, frequency and phase, often fed by reflected-power sensing.
technologies.performance: Solid-state systems claim >70% efficiency vs ~45-50% for magnetrons and >15-yr device life vs ~5,000-h magnetron warranty; enable automatic power matching under load variation
technologies.limits: Hardware capex, not software; benefits materialize only when combined with an operating model telling it what to do; retrofit business case still developing

technologies.name: Incumbent baseline: operator heuristics + OEM service contracts + trial-and-error
technologies.how: Operators tune power/belt speed/recipe empirically; OEMs provide occasional optimization visits; universities/consultants run one-off studies.
technologies.performance: Zero software cost but leaves 10-30% energy/quality upside unrealized; microwave drying studies report up to ~30% energy savings and up to ~80% shorter drying times vs conventional tunnels when properly optimized
technologies.limits: Knowledge leaves with retiring specialists; empiricism cannot see inside the cavity (hot spots, arcing risk, runaway); inconsistent across batches/materials

tech_baseline.why_better_text: Incumbents fail this hypothesis in two directions: generalist EM tools can compute the physics but require experts the operators do not employ, and generic digital-twin platforms reach the operator but are blind to microwave physics. A domain-focused tool built on ProSeed's microwave know-how — pre-modelled machine/applicator templates, a validated dielectric database, and operator-facing KPIs (energy per kg product, uniformity index, runaway margin) — can deliver simulation-driven setpoint optimization without requiring an RF engineer on staff. ProSeed can also pair the software with retrofit sensing (reflected-power, temperature) so models self-calibrate on the real machine, something neither simulation vendors nor twin platforms currently do.
key_assumptions: Global installed base of industrial microwave process machines is ~10^4-10^5 units (assumed; anchored to ~$1.4-1.6B/yr equipment sales and SAIREM's disclosed ~5,000 installed machines alone)
Industrial microwaves in Europe consume ~9.6 TWh/yr and typical magnetron systems run at ~45-50% wall-to-load efficiency vs >70% claimed for solid-state (measured, EU H2020 CLEAN-HEAT)

Realistic efficiency/quality gain from simulation-guided operation is ~10-30% energy and less scrap/hot-spot damage (assumed; supported by reported ~30% tunnel-dryer savings and dielectric-sensitivity literature)
Operators will not hire RF specialists: product must be usable by process engineers, which caps acceptable complexity (assumed)

Per-site value requires measured dielectric/thermal data of the actual product — a service-heavy calibration step that limits pure-SaaS scalability (assumed, consistent with literature emphasis on temperature-dependent dielectric data scarcity)
